newsitem.title: USA: Caribbean airports jammed ahead of strike deadline.
newsitem.headline: Caribbean airports jammed ahead of strike deadline.

text.p: Caribbean airports were jammed on Friday, as travelers scrambled to reach vacation spots or return home ahead of a midnight strike deadline at American Airlines.

In a scene reminiscent of the hours before a vicious summer hurricane, nervous travelers clutched tickets and pleaded with agents to give them seats on flights departing before a pilots' walkout set for 12:01 a.m. EST (0501 GMT) on Saturday.
"I'm scared," said New Jersey resident Rita Thomas, a tourist on St. Thomas in the U.S. Virgin Islands. "I have to get out next Wednesday."

"This has ruined my Valentine's Day. My heart is broken." said Natasha Civil, a teacher stranded in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, where American is the only major passenger airline. She was counting on flying to New York to see her boy friend.
American controls an estimated 70 percent of the air travel into the Caribbean, and hotel owners have estimated a strike could cost them $15 million per day.

Tourism officials nervously worked to minimise the slowdown in business at the region's resorts on the long U.S. Presidents Day weekend, considered one of the most important travel periods of the year.
Others appealed to President Bill Clinton to intervene.
In Jamaica, Gordon "Butch" Stewart, the chairman of Air Jamaica and the Sandals chain of resorts, urged the White House to force the airline and its pilots to submit to binding arbitration.
A strike "would be likened to the destruction which would accompany a massive hurricane hitting every single island at the same time," Stewart said.

On St. Thomas, St. Croix and St. John, travelers with tickets on American Airlines were given incentives to take their vacations, including the promise of full refunds by large hotels if they could not use their tickets, and credits from hotels with fewer than 50 guest rooms.
"The strategy is to keep people from not making reservations or from panicking and cancelling the reservations they already have," said government spokeswoman Amy Atkinson.

Throughout the Caribbean tourism officials turned into travel agents, who were negotiating with charter companies to provide flights from New York and Miami to the islands in case of a prolonged American strike.

"It is possible that this strike will affect us for one or two days, but no more," said Dominican Republic Minister of Tourism Felix Jimenez, whose nation is one of the most vulnerable to an American strike.
The airline has a 72 percent market share in Santo Domingo, a 66 percent share at the airport at Puerto Plata, a resort area, and flights to other areas of the country.

"We're not in a very good mood right now," Alison Daly said, after speaking to an American ticket agent at Miami International Airport, where thousands of travelers each day transfer to American's Latin American and Caribbean flights.
Daly and her husband's flight from Newark, New Jersey, to Miami was delayed and they missed their connection to the Dominican resort of La Romana, where American is the only air carrier.

The ticket agent offered the couple few options: They could fly back to chilly Newark, stay in Miami and try to get out Saturday, or fly to San Juan, Puerto Rico, and try to get to the Dominican Republic from there -- the latter two options involving air trips after the strike was due to begin.
"I don't know what we are going to do," Daly said.
But there were a few people who were not unhappy with the possibility of a few extra days in the tropics.
"We hope to get stranded here," said Nancy Langley, who was enjoying the balmy weather in St. Thomas on Friday.
She expressed no longing to return home to Boston, where temperatures were just above freezing.
